entry.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

link.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

entry.content:
For my internship I left my UCLA computational chemistry desk for a while and joined SES AI, a battery company, as an Applied Scientist intern, and followed one question up three scales: molecules, the electrolytes they make up, and the cells those electrolytes go into. Along the way I taught models to read molecules off real paper figures (59.8% exact on 331 journal figures), to watch about 40,000 molecular-dynamics movies of electrolytes, and to learn how a battery cell ages step by step instead of guessing one lifetime number. This post is the map; the three parts are the territory.

The one question

The official title I gave the work was “multiscale multimodal intelligence across molecules, electrolytes, and cells,” which is a mouthful, so here’s the version I’d tell you over coffee. Today’s AI models are very good with pictures and text. They can describe a cat photo and write a poem about it. But chemistry and batteries don’t really live in pictures and text. They live in 3D geometry, where atoms actually sit in space; in physical time, how those atoms jiggle, drift and react over nanoseconds to months; and in scales that connect, where a tiny change in one molecule shows up, much later, as a battery that lasts longer (or doesn’t).

So the question I kept asking all internship was whether AI can understand not just pictures and text, but 3D geometry, physical time, and how the scales connect.

Three scales, one storyline

The storyline follows the stuff itself: molecules make up electrolytes, and electrolytes go into cells. Think of a battery like a city. The molecules are the people. The electrolyte is the crowd, the liquid the ions swim through, made of salt, solvents and additives. The cell is the whole city, with its traffic jams, heat waves and aging infrastructure. You can’t understand a city from one person’s ID card, and you can’t understand a crowd without watching it move, so the work split into three parts, each building on the last.

I kept redrawing the project map all summer. The left side is molecules, from paper drawings to 3D geometry and energies. The right side is electrolytes, from quantum reference data to force fields, and from 40K MD trajectories to learned representations, both feeding an electrolyte co-scientist.

Part 1: molecules, the foundation

Part 1 starts from a plain problem: right now, mostly humans can read the molecule drawings in papers, and papers draw the same molecule in a dozen outfits, sometimes by hand. A chemist shrugs and says “atom is atom, bond is bond.” A model trained on neat, computer-rendered drawings panics.

I post-trained vision-language models to read real paper figures and found that the real bottleneck is the gap between rendered and real images. I built VERDICT, four independent readers that would rather say “I’m not sure” than make something up, and a rotation-aware recognizer that knows a rotated drawing is the same molecule but a mirrored one might not be. Then I turned recognized molecules into vectors, using 1D, 2D and 3D descriptions, five public base models and three kinds of training, and asked honestly what 3D really adds.

It all ends in a truly multimodal database, delivered through the MU product and a Chrome extension: start from a molecule picture and jump to what the paper says, its DFT properties, or its MD properties. Read it here: Atom is atom, bond is bond.

Part 2: electrolytes, molecules mixed into a liquid

Part 2 takes the molecules from Part 1 and makes them the salt, solvents and additives of an electrolyte, which looks like a boring puddle and is really a dance floor. Lithium ions grab solvent partners, anions cut in, everything shuffles.

To simulate that dance you need a rulebook, a force field, and a movie projector, molecular dynamics. I extended a polarizable force field (PFF) to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, got humbled when fits that looked perfect on small clusters made the liquid clump (more than 50 of 80 versions failed), and distilled those failures into PFF RSI, a fitting loop that turns every saved mistake into an automatic check.

Then I taught a model to watch about 40,000 of these movies through three heads: the recipe (what’s in the bottle), a snapshot (one frozen frame of atoms) and the trajectory (how everything moves over time), all compressed into one shared 128-number space used for retrieval, alignment and property prediction.

Finally, I curated everything I’d learned (task records, simulation logs and bugs, tool definitions) to fine-tune an open-weight LLM and put it inside a harness of tools and checks: an electrolyte co-scientist that explains failed runs and prepares new ones, with a researcher reviewing what it proposes. Read it here: Teaching a puddle to dance.

Part 3: cells, electrolytes inside batteries

Part 3 puts the electrolyte formulations from Part 2 into cells and reaches the question everyone at a battery company actually cares about: if I change the recipe, say by adding an additive, what happens to the battery? Does it cycle longer, store better, charge faster?

The central idea is that nothing from Parts 1 and 2 gets thrown away. Both were mostly representation learning, so a cell can be represented by stacking the learned molecule representations and the electrolyte latent, with the cell’s design and conditions on top. Real experiments are slow and expensive, so around a 252-formulation additive experiment I built a ladder of simulations, one rung per scale: from electrons (DFT) to the liquid (MD), to bonds breaking at the electrode surface (interface reactions), to how that surface evolves over long times (kMC), to voltage, capacity and aging (P2D / SPMe), all the way up to temperature and stress across the whole cell (3D fields). Then I aligned those scales in one shared space and found that test conditions are the glue that holds them together.

The part I’m most excited about is the aging world model. Instead of a black box that predicts lifetime as one number, it learns the whole evolution process: given the cell’s design, its current state and how it’s being used, predict the next state, and roll that forward into a full aging curve. Learning the process rather than the endpoint is also where I started to see what I’d call knowledge emergence, which I’m still working to confirm properly.

It ends with a cell co-scientist that reasons over representations from all three parts, plus a decision API that hands the agent’s small, repetitive judgment calls to a typed decision model so the reasoning model can focus on reasoning. Read it here: From molecules to batteries.

The same four steps at every scale

Only when I laid the three parts side by side did I notice they follow the same four steps: represent, align, predict, and hand the result to a co-scientist. For molecules, that’s VLMs and VERDICT reading drawings plus 1D/2D/3D representations, aligned views, property prediction, and the multimodal database. For electrolytes, it’s three heads into a 128-d latent, then properties, then the electrolyte co-scientist. For cells, it’s stacked representations and multiscale alignment, then regression and classification heads plus the world model, then the cell co-scientist.

One lesson also kept showing up at every scale: a pretty number on the training objective is not the same as the scientific goal. A preference model can score beautifully and still get molecules wrong. A force field can nail tiny clusters and still ruin the liquid. An alignment can match molecules perfectly and still say almost nothing about real batteries. So most of my summer was spent building the checks: agreement between independent readers, liquid simulations inside the fitting loop, calibration against real measurements. Less glamorous than a leaderboard, but it’s what lets you trust the answer.

What this got us

I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin; the method should transfer to most systems like them, the ones built as molecules, then mixtures, then devices, where the important structure lives in drawings, geometry and simulations rather than text, and where experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. It’s still a living method, and I keep adding pieces as the field moves. Grab a snack: Part 1 starts at the foundation, with a molecule and a computer trying to figure out who it is.
entry.summary: Overview of a three-part series on my Applied Scientist internship at SES AI: molecules make up electrolytes, electrolytes go into batteries, and each part builds on the representations of the one before

entry.title: From molecules to batteries
entry.content:
The electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real cells here, and the question becomes the one a battery company actually cares about: if I change the recipe, what changes in the battery? Starting from 252 additive-centered formulations, I stacked the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 into a cell representation, built a ladder of multiscale simulations around the real recipes, aligned the scales, trained an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and wrapped it all in a cell co-scientist. The clearest finding was that test conditions are the glue between scales: removing them collapsed a key cross-scale link score from 0.327 to 0.066.

Δrecipe → Δperformance

My starting point was a real, specific problem: a design of experiments (DOE) of 252 cell formulations built around additives, and a lot of questions about it. Within each comparison the electrodes were held fixed and the additives changed, so any change in performance can be pinned on the recipe. The question is simple to say: change the recipe, and what changes in capacity retention, cycle life, resistance and rate? On my slides that’s cycling, storage, charging and rate.

It’s a bit like baking. Swap one ingredient and the cake might rise higher, or collapse, or taste fine today and go stale next month. The annoying part is that each real bake for a battery is slow and expensive, and there was no budget for repeated new rounds of experiments. Compute, on the other hand, was available. So the plan was to use compute to fill in around the real data, while real measurements stay the reference. Simulations get to advise; they don’t get to overrule.

A cell is a stack of representations

The idea that unlocked this part is that nothing from Parts 1 and 2 had to be thrown away. Both were, underneath the jokes, a lot of representation learning. Part 1 turned every molecule into vectors from its 1D, 2D and 3D views. Part 2 turned every electrolyte into 128 numbers in a shared latent space, learned from recipes, snapshots and trajectories. A battery cell can be represented by stacking those learned pieces: the molecule representations for each component, the electrolyte latent for the mixture, and the cell’s own design and operating conditions on top.

Scales stacking up into a cell, like Lego bricks that were secretly designed to fit together. The storyline of the series is that molecules make up electrolytes and electrolytes go into cells, and here the representations follow the same path.

A ladder of simulations around the real recipes

A stack of representations needs something to learn from, and 252 formulations is not a lot, so I spent about a month building a high-throughput ladder of high-fidelity simulations around the DOE itself: around its real recipes and its real test protocols, not around made-up chemistry. No single simulation covers everything from electrons to a whole cell heating up, so each rung hands something to the next.

Here are the six rungs, in the order on my slides.

  1. DFT looks at electrons and local chemistry: whether an additive can be reduced, who coordinates around the ion, and how much energy it takes for a molecule to decompose. That local chemistry is the starting point for the liquid.
  2. MD shows how molecules organize and move in the liquid: solvation, aggregation, diffusion and conductivity. This is the PFF from Part 2, back for an encore, and it supplies what arrives at the electrode.
  3. Interface reactions ask how molecules may change near the electrode, the battery’s busiest border crossing, where bonds break and form; I explored these with a learned force model, and the events it finds become the moves for the next rung.
  4. kMC (kinetic Monte Carlo) thinks in states, events and rates, like a board game where each move happens with some probability per unit time, to ask what happens next over long times. When I compressed MD transport into 12 states, the model’s held-out transition NLL was 1.612 versus 2.273 for an independent-state baseline (lower is better). Full SEI growth was not validated, so I’m not claiming it. On the slide, kMC sits inside the cell model, which is the next rung.
  5. P2D and SPMe model the whole cell’s transport and reactions: voltage, capacity and aging. P2D resolves what happens through the electrode’s thickness and inside its particles; SPMe is its simpler, cheaper cousin for when you need many runs fast. Both treat the cell as one stack, so the last rung spreads it out in space.
  6. 3D fields capture temperature and stress varying across the cell. I ran 3,331 electrothermal simulations linked to DOE records, using the recorded protocols, with stated assumptions about geometry and thermal inputs.

Every calculation keeps its recipe, conditions, source and a fidelity label: measured, calculated or predicted. Mixing those up is how you end up trusting a simulation more than the experiment it was supposed to explain.

Lining up the scales

With simulations at every scale, the next step was to connect them, the same way Part 2 connected recipes, frames and motion. Each input got its own encoder, mapped into a shared 128-d space. Then I learned links between neighboring scales: DFT ↔ molecules, molecules ↔ formulations, formulations + conditions ↔ MD, MD + conditions ↔ cells, cells + conditions ↔ DOE, plus links for the interface. The loss was a multi-positive InfoNCE, a fancy way of saying “pull together everything that belongs to the same experiment, push apart everything that doesn’t,” along with predicting the next scale’s vector from the current one.

To keep myself honest I trained four versions, three seeds each: the full model, no conditions, shuffled pairs, and no extra linking loss. Two findings stood out. The first is that conditions are the glue. Temperature, C-rate and protocol are what connect the scales: removing them collapsed the MD-to-electrode link score from 0.327 to 0.066. Without knowing how a battery was tested, the scales stop recognizing each other. Correct pairs also scored much better than shuffled ones, so the links are real.

The second finding is that molecules don’t get you to a battery just via alignment. Matching a molecule’s identity across views could be strong while the links to the real DOE stayed weaker. Knowing exactly who someone is doesn’t tell you how they’ll do at their new job.

On top of the shared space sit regression and classification heads for property prediction. With chemistry inputs only, the normalized error (MAE across DOE targets) fell from 0.3341 to 0.2849 using modality dropout, which means randomly hiding inputs during training so the model learns to cope when some are missing. It cost a little when every input was available (0.2442 → 0.2542), a trade I’ll happily take. And the uncertainty was overconfident: nominal 90% intervals covered only about 68–78%. When the model said “I’m 90% sure,” it should have said “eh, maybe 70%.” Good to know, and now it’s written down.

From one number to the whole story: an aging world model

The heads still predict a target as one number, and that’s the habit this section breaks: the goal shifted from predicting lifetime to learning the whole evolution process, how the cell’s state evolves under its design and its conditions. The usual black box takes the recipe in and gives one number out (“lifetime: N cycles”). It gives you nothing to check along the way, and when it’s wrong, it can’t tell you why.

To learn a process you need to watch it happen many times, and real experiments are few and slow. Simulations, on the other hand, give dense, state-by-state trajectories under many designs and conditions. So I ran a large number of P2D and 3D aging simulations: expensive, long DFN (full P2D) runs for some cases and cheaper, short SPMe runs for many more, screening early and recording why each run stopped. The 3D layer added 100,000 electrothermal entries and 200,000 chemical-mechanical results. The DOE stays the real-cell reference throughout.

The world model works like this. Given the cell’s design, its current state (voltage, capacity, temperature, aging variables, state of health) and the condition (how it’s being used: protocol, temperature, C-rate), it predicts the next state. Then it rolls out: each prediction becomes the next input, step by step, into a full aging curve, and the lifetime is read off where the curve hits an endpoint, for example 80% of initial capacity. The same machinery covers calendar aging (sitting on a shelf) and cycle aging (being used). It’s like predicting tomorrow’s weather, then using that forecast to predict the day after.

I compared 41 architectures on an early dataset of 6,258 simulated sequences × 140 steps, and the learned world model beat a direct MLP baseline on simulated sequences. My historical summary recorded roughly 24–27% lower error. I haven’t yet traced every one of those numbers back to its fold and target, and to be very clear, it is a lower prediction error on simulations, not an increase in anyone’s real cycle life.

Each world model faces four checks: next-step accuracy; long-run drift, which is harsh because small errors snowball; the direction of change when you swap an additive or a condition; and agreement with real experiments. The honest gap is that a model that learns the simulator very well can also inherit the simulator’s mistakes. How well it learns the simulations and how well it matches real cells are separate questions.

Here’s the part that got me most excited, and I want to be careful with it. Because the model learns the process instead of memorizing endpoints, I started to see it pick up physically sensible chemistry and battery behavior that nobody spelled out for it, which is what I’d call knowledge emergence. That’s my observation and interpretation, not a measured result. What I can point to is how it gets checked: rollouts are inspected for unphysical behavior in capacity, temperature and concentration at different horizons, held-out operating conditions test whether the model responds in the right direction, and the direction-of-change check is one of the four tests above. I’m not claiming it discovered anything specific like SEI growth or lithium plating. Confirming emergence rigorously is ongoing work, and probably my favorite open question from the summer.

Checking against real cells

Simulations are the practice field, not the match, so the last scientific step was to hold the models up against the DOE. My favorite plot twist came from one additive, VC. In matched DOE comparisons it hurt cycle life in one cell design and helped in another. Same ingredient, opposite story. A physics model built on a fixed VC-SEI hypothesis reproduced some of the sign changes, but not the full direction and size of the effect.

That sounds like a failure, but it’s the most useful kind of result: it turns the hypothesis into a candidate mechanism with a concrete next test. It also comes with a rule I try hard to follow: don’t tune a model on the DOE and then hold up the same DOE as validation. That’s grading your own homework with the answer key taped to the back. The bridge between simulation and reality is calibration against real experiments, and the sim-to-real calibration supported 24 targets. Everything else stays labeled for what it is: simulated until a real cell says otherwise.

A cell co-scientist

The last piece was the same move as at the end of Part 2, one scale up: hand everything to a co-scientist that can reason over it. This time the inputs come from every level. In the early version, each record carried 396 molecular features (Part 1), 274 electrolyte features (Part 2) and 105 cell features (this part), 775 numbers in all. Each group goes through its own small projector into 4 “soft tokens,” and the 12 soft prefix tokens sit in front of the text, with missing inputs masked. Tokenization is chemistry-aware: common molecule names are kept as single tokens, with markers for chemistry and scale, so names get read as chemistry rather than letter soup.

Next to the numbers goes text evidence: the recipe, the conditions, measured and simulated results, and where each came from. I also built explanation examples from evidence packages: a teacher model writes the explanation, and a critic plus fixed rules check it. A first pilot had 300 examples covering complete, missing, novel and conflicting evidence. On top of that come the data, the simulation logs and the tool-usage records. Held-out experimental answers stayed out of training, forward prediction can’t see the target value, and the split is by recipe. The fine-tuning itself is LoRA (QLoRA) on the LLM, trained together with the scientific projectors.

The harness is DeepSeek Harness, connected to battery tools: cell prediction, recipe suggestions, similar experiments, cross-scale explanations, multiscale evidence, and formulation comparison, plus a call to the trained specialist that attaches the record’s evidence chain. A workspace keeps the conversation, the explanations and the tool history. The work is split between two models: a larger LLM handles planning and tool calls, and the fine-tuned compact open-weight LLM acts as the scientific specialist. Its training data didn’t include tool-call trajectories, and I learned that good scientific answers don’t automatically give you reliable tool use.

So what can it do? It connects recipes, conditions, simulated states and measurements; explains an answer with sources; compares candidate formulations; suggests recipes; finds similar experiments; and says what evidence is missing and what the next useful calculation would be. The interface shows the explanation, the tool calls, the returned results and the record IDs, and it marks every piece of evidence as measured, computed, predicted, missing or rejected. If you’ve read this far, you know why that matters to me. To be honest about where it stands: in the demo, prediction and inverse design still used DOE retrieval and ranking of measured recipes, and connecting the world model is further work. A first explanation-training pilot didn’t improve the combined score, so it stayed experimental. And the reasoning text it writes is an output to inspect, not proof of what happened inside the model.

Watching the agent work gave me one more idea, which is design thinking rather than a measured result. A lot of what an agent does all day is small and repetitive: is this record relevant, which of these four candidates fits, how complete is this evidence on a five-level scale. Those steps need judgment or a score, not long reasoning, and they’re exactly where a general LLM can wander off and return something malformed. So I’d route them through a decision API to Jev, TypeSafe AI’s decision model, released on 15 September 2026 as a “System One” decision model. Jev answers typed questions about a text or JSON state and only returns structured outputs: a Choice (pick from up to 255 options, with probabilities), a Score (a position on a rubric of 2 to 10 levels that you describe), or a yes/no probability. An independent evaluation reports 95–99% accuracy on several classification benchmarks and well-calibrated choice probabilities. Its “can’t hallucinate” guarantee is about format: the output always matches the declared schema, so no invented options and no parse errors. It isn’t a guarantee of correctness, and it can still pick a valid but wrong answer, which is why those steps still get checked. The point of the split is that the small judgments never come back malformed and come with calibrated probabilities, and the reasoning LLM is freed to do what it’s good at, which should make the whole agent stronger.

I’d like to say this is now a finished method of my own: represent, align, predict, then a co-scientist with a decision API. Honestly, the field moves so fast that I spent the summer chasing the frontier and bolting new pieces on, and I expect to keep doing that. It’s a living method, and this is its current version.

What this got us

The summer followed the stuff itself. Molecules got recognized and represented (Part 1), mixed into electrolytes whose rulebook, movies and latent space I built (Part 2), and went into cells, where the representations stacked up, the scales got aligned, a world model learned how the whole thing ages, and a co-scientist learned to reason over all of it (Part 3). Looking back, the same pattern showed up at every scale: represent, align, predict, and hand it to a co-scientist. I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin, and I think the pieces add up to a framework that should transfer to similar systems: complex material and chemical systems built as molecules, then mixtures or formulations, then devices, where the structure lives in non-text data like drawings, geometry, trajectories and simulations, the scales are linked by conditions, and experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. Through all of it, real experiments stayed the reference: simulations explore, models propose, measurements decide. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have a mechanism test to think about.
entry.summary: Part 3, cells: the electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real batteries, and the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 stack up into a representation of the cell. Multiscale simulations around a 252-formulation experiment, alignment between scales, an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and a cell co-scientist that closes the series

entry.title: Teaching a puddle to dance
entry.content:
In Part 1 molecules got recognized and turned into vectors; here they get mixed into electrolytes, and the question becomes how they move. I extended a polarizable force field (PFF) to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, watched more than 50 of 80 versions fail once they had to behave as a liquid, turned those failures into a self-improving fitting loop called PFF RSI, and taught a model to read about 40,000 molecular-dynamics movies through three heads and one shared 128-number space. That space predicts conductivity with R² 0.976, trajectory features improved conductivity error in 18 of 21 held-out chemistry groups, and everything I learned along the way became training material for an electrolyte co-scientist.

How do molecules move in a liquid?

The question on my slides for this part was “how do molecules move in their micro-environment?”, and it starts with what an electrolyte actually is. An electrolyte is the liquid inside a battery that ions swim through. The recipe is simple: salt + solvents + additives, and those are exactly the molecules from Part 1, now with jobs. The behavior is not simple. Zoom in and it’s a crowded dance floor: lithium ions grab solvent molecules as partners, anions try to cut in, and how fast everyone gets across the floor decides how well the battery charges and discharges.

To watch that dance on a computer you need two things. A force field is the rulebook for how atoms push and pull on each other. Molecular dynamics (MD) is playing the movie with that rulebook: put lots of molecules in a box, apply the rules, and watch. If the rulebook is wrong, the movie is fiction. Very confident, beautifully rendered fiction.

Writing a bigger rulebook

My first job was to grow the rulebook so that the molecules people actually want to try have rules to follow. The force field is polarizable, meaning electron clouds can squish in response to their neighbors, which matters a lot around small, charged ions like lithium. The goal was coverage: extend it to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, for both lithium and sodium electrolytes.

The reference data comes from quantum chemistry (DFT), and lots of it. Some clusters are binary: the ion with one partner. Some are ternary: a solvent and an anion competing for the same ion, like two people reaching for the last slice of pizza. Each pair or trio gets computed at many distances and orientations, so the rulebook sees close calls, near misses and awkward side-on approaches, not just the polite pose.

What I fit was mainly the exp-6 cross terms, keeping the charges and the polarization background fixed. Exp-6 is the part of the rulebook that covers short-range repulsion (“personal space!”) and dispersion, the weak, sticky attraction between everything. The “exp” is an exponential wall that keeps atoms from overlapping; the “6” is a gentle pull that falls off with the sixth power of distance. All the while I was debugging, learning electrolyte science on the fly, and studying the properties that came out. Three jobs at once, which is roughly how every internship works.

The liquid gets a vote

The hardest lesson of the summer was that a fit isn’t done when the cluster error is low; it’s done when the liquid behaves. Density, radial distribution functions (who stands next to whom), diffusion, conductivity and viscosity all have to come out sensible in MD. My ledger ended up indexing 80 distinct force-field versions, and more than 50 of them failed. Here are a few of my favorite ways to fail.

One fit looked great on the clusters. Errors low, curves lined up, very satisfying. Then I ran the liquid and it clumped: the ions huddled together like penguins in a blizzard. I traced it to one ether-oxygen interaction the fit had effectively broken. Restoring it cut the ion aggregation fraction from 0.811 to 0.282, and from 0.415 to 0.044 in a second system. Conductivity moved closer to experiment, though it was still too low. Progress, not victory.

Another time, a tiny coefficient, 0.00170, got rounded to zero on its way into the simulation. The builder treated zero as “missing” and helpfully swapped a big repulsive wall for a small one, and MD failed. Now a check reads the final built parameters, not just the ones I meant to build. And in my favorite, lone-pair virtual sites stored with the label “He” were passed to DFT as real helium atoms. That quietly affected 27 of 61 clusters. Nothing says summer internship like accidentally inventing noble-gas electrolyte chemistry. Now templates, masses and site types are checked before anything goes out.

One failure was actually a success. A salt-free solvent control came out at a viscosity of about 2.1–2.4 mPa·s, which told me the solvent was fine and the problem lived in the salt model. The lesson I now believe in my bones: a low DFT fitting error doesn’t protect the liquid, and MD validation is part of parameter development, not a final demo.

PFF RSI: turning failures into checks

Fifty-odd failures is a lot of pain, but it’s also a lot of data, so I distilled them into a recursive self-improvement system, PFF RSI. The slide version is a simple cycle: fit the force field, validate in MD, record the failures, refine the next fit.

Underneath the cycle, the slide stacks four layers: context, memory, code harness and weights. A saved failure is memory: the system, the version, what changed, what I expected versus what I measured, and what it cost, stored so it can be searched later by conditions, bad parameters, symptoms and useful checks. Loading the relevant failures before a new fit is context. Turning a failure into an automatic check is a new procedure, written as code in the harness, so the same mistake gets caught by a machine instead of by me at 11 pm. The weights are the fitted parameters that the whole loop keeps refining.

When a brand-new molecule shows up, the loop runs on its own. It samples a small starting set of clusters and expands only the channels that failed, fits, and checks. Parameters that match a known failure pattern get intercepted and sent to MD for a look before anyone uses them, so the wall that rounded to zero and the helium incident can’t sneak through twice. The honest caveat is that a fixed-budget test proving this memory actually makes research faster is still on my to-do list. It feels faster. Feelings aren’t data.

40,000 movies and three heads

Once the rulebook works you can make movies, lots of them, and then you hit a new problem: none of it is text. Each trajectory is 5,000 frames, one every 4 picoseconds, for 20 nanoseconds in total. I ended up with about 40,000 trajectories, roughly 200 million frames.

You can’t paste a trajectory into a chatbot and ask how it felt. It’s coordinates, boxes and time, and the interesting part (who solvates whom, how ions hop) is spread across thousands of frames. So I asked whether a model could learn what a liquid is by watching, and squeeze each one into something small enough to search, compare and predict with. I looked at the same liquid through three views, each with its own encoder, or “head,” in the same order as my slides.

The recipe encoder reads what’s in the bottle: the components, their amounts, and conditions like temperature, and turns them into 128 numbers. The snapshot encoder reads one frame of 3D atoms; it’s my favorite, so it gets its own section below. The trajectory encoder reads motion over time: the 5,000 frames are split into 50 chunks of 100, so the model sees how things move, not just a pose.

All three are compressed into one shared 128-d latent space and trained with three-way contrastive alignment: views of the same liquid are pulled together, views of different liquids pushed apart. A recipe should find its own movie, and a snapshot should find its own recipe. That one space then does three jobs: retrieval, alignment between views, and property prediction.

For retrieval, retrieval@10 (is the matching liquid in the top 10?) was 84.1% with the full representation versus 82.4% from the static snapshot alone, so a single frame already knows a lot. For conductivity, the model reached R² 0.976, close to a strong descriptor baseline, and adding trajectory features improved conductivity error in 18 of 21 held-out chemistry groups: motion helps, especially on chemistry the model hasn’t seen. On my summary slide the property heads came out at R² 0.906, 0.936 and 0.987 for conductivity, viscosity and solubility. One more finding I’m fond of: the representation carried over from lithium to sodium electrolytes with only a simple alignment step. Same dance, different lead dancer.

From there the slides go two steps further. Reverse design starts from the properties you want and looks for recipes that land there. I also tried trajectory generation, rolling the movie forward with GRU, TCN and causal-transformer models, which I’ll leave as a teaser.

Inside the snapshot encoder

The snapshot encoder is where the physics goes into the architecture, the same way rotation did in Part 1. Each frame becomes a periodic atom graph: every atom connects to neighbors within 6 Å, using the minimum-image rule across the box boundaries (the box wraps around like Pac-Man), and whole molecules are kept intact instead of getting sliced at the edge.

Then comes equivariant message passing. Each atom carries two kinds of luggage: plain numbers (scalars) and little arrows (vectors). Messages are built from distances and directions, so when you rotate the box, the arrows rotate right along with it and the final pooled numbers don’t change at all. The model doesn’t waste effort learning that a rotated liquid is the same liquid (the same “atom is atom” spirit as Part 1), while still keeping directional information like which way a solvent faces a lithium ion. Each frame comes out as 128 learned numbers plus 8 geometric ones, such as lithium coordination and ion contacts: 136 numbers per frame.

Then the unglamorous part, which made everything else possible. Neighbor search went from O(N²) to O(N): instead of every atom asking every other atom “are you close?”, each atom only checks its own neighborhood. Then I froze the encoder and cached about 192 million snapshots once, which took 395 H200 GPU-hours and a cache of about 52 GB. After that, a training step went from 12.6 s to 0.15 s. That’s the difference between “let’s try an idea” and “let’s try an idea next week.”

The electrolyte co-scientist

Everything above is how I came to understand formulation, and the last step was to hand that understanding to something that could use it. So I curated it into training material. The first part is organized scientific task records: formulation and MD cases, reading evidence, a public conductivity dataset (CALiSol), and policy examples, 254,527 rows in the model’s chat and tool format (rows are tasks, not independent formulations). The second is the MD engine’s simulation logs, bugs and failures; the helium incident lives on. The third is tool-usage records plus the tool definitions themselves.

I fine-tuned an open-weight LLM with LoRA for about one epoch, 63,632 steps on one GPU. Fine-tuning teaches the model the task format, how to read evidence, and when and how to call tools. It does not turn the model into a calculator: the numbers still come from the data and the programs.

The harness does the rest. It has a tool registry (file reading, protocol checks, analysis programs, evidence records, and PFF RSI itself) and a loop: the researcher asks, the LLM plans, and the harness retrieves experiments, calls the explanation and generation models, executes approved simulations, and compares results with saved artifacts. Preparing a run is kept separate from submitting it. A request carries the formulation, protocol, resources and a fingerprint, gets validated before a job is ever created, is recognized if it’s a repeat (no burning GPU time on the same run twice), and can recover after a failure. Raw trajectories stay on the tool side; the LLM sees summaries, not 5,000 frames of coordinates.

The tools had their own growing pains, and I fixed three I’m proud of. An unsupported unit used to look like “no data,” so the model would conclude nothing existed; now the tool rejects it clearly. Short error messages made the model guess over and over, like someone jiggling a locked door; now errors spell out the full argument contract. And one request passed every numeric check while “DMC” was carrying the SMILES of DMF, a different molecule with a confusingly similar name; now the checker verifies chemical identity, which is Part 1’s lesson coming back to collect.

So what can it do? It can explain why a simulation failed, how a formulation performed, or how to prepare a run at a new temperature, and the researcher stays in charge by reviewing the next formulations it proposes. This was also when I noticed I was building a way of working more than a single model: represent the liquid, align its views, predict, then hand it to a co-scientist. I’d love to call that a method of my own, but the field moves so fast that I kept adding new pieces to it all summer, so for now it’s a living one.

What this got us

Part 2 gave us a rulebook that covers the molecules people want to try and that learns from its own mistakes, a 128-number description of each liquid learned from recipes, frames and motion, and a co-scientist that knows how to read all of it. Nobody buys a puddle, though. These formulations only matter once they’re sealed inside a real battery, next to electrodes, getting charged and discharged for months, and that’s where Part 3 takes them.
entry.summary: Part 2, electrolytes: the molecules recognized and represented in Part 1 become the salt, solvents and additives of a liquid. Extending a polarizable force field, a fitting loop that learns from its own failures, three heads that compress 40,000 molecular movies into one latent space, and an electrolyte co-scientist trained on all of it

entry.title: Atom is atom, bond is bond

link.title: Atom is atom, bond is bond

entry.content:
Molecules are where this series starts, because electrolytes are mixtures of molecules and batteries are built around electrolytes, so before anything else a computer has to look at a molecule drawn in a paper and know who it is. I post-trained vision-language models to read real paper figures, built VERDICT to check their answers by letting four independent readers vote (and abstain), tried a rotation-aware recognizer, and then turned the recognized molecules into vectors and a multimodal database. The best model read 59.8% of 331 real journal figures exactly, on par with a strong established reader, and agreement between readers separated right answers from wrong ones with an AUROC of 0.916.

Only people can read the drawings

The problem I started from is that a lot of chemistry is locked inside drawings that only people can read. Papers and patents are full of molecule figures. A chemist glances at one and says “ah, FEC.” A computer sees pixels. As long as that’s the case, every molecule in the literature has to be found by someone squinting at a PDF. If you want to search by structure, or pull every molecule a paper tested into a database, you need recognition that a computer can do at high throughput. And not only for neat drawings: people sketch molecules by hand, too.

The catch is that papers draw the same molecule in wildly different styles: thin double bonds, atom labels the size of a dust mite, wedge bonds, scans that look like they went through a fax machine twice.

My slides tell this as a little comic. Cartoon me holds up a drawing and asks the model “who are you?”, and the right answer is “NaPF6 in FEC.” A chemist looks at every outfit above and shrugs with the line that became my motto for the summer: atom is atom, bond is bond. The style doesn’t matter. The model, at first, disagreed.

To teach it, I had two kinds of training data. Synthetic drawings are free and endless: chemistry software (RDKit, RDKit-coordgen, Indigo, RanDepict) can render any molecule in many styles. Real drawings are scarcer and messier: USPTO patent figures, UOB, and DECIMER-HDM, a set of hand-drawn molecules.

Here’s the trap. Because synthetic drawings are endless, it’s easy to train a model that looks amazing on them. But the real bottleneck wasn’t the amount of data. It was distribution shift: the gap between tidy rendered training images and messy real paper figures. A model can ace the rendered exam and still flunk the real world. Most of my summer on molecules went into three attempts at closing that gap.

Post-training a vision-language model

My first attempt was to take a general vision-language model and post-train it to read molecule drawings. A vision-language model (VLM) looks at an image and writes text about it. Inside, an image encoder (a ViT) chops the picture into patches and turns them into vectors, a small projector translates those vectors into the language model’s space, and the language model writes the answer. Here the answer is a SMILES string, a line of text that spells out the molecule atom by atom.

I compared three public base models, GLM-4.1V-9B, InternVL3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, across six mixtures of real and synthetic images, using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with LoRA. LoRA is the “don’t renovate the whole house, just add a small extension” approach: instead of changing every weight in a big model, you learn small low-rank updates next to the frozen weights. My recipe was LoRA rank 16, BF16 numbers, small batches, activation checkpointing (recompute some things instead of storing them, to save memory), and selective adaptation of the vision part. Unglamorous, but it fits on the hardware.

To keep myself honest, I split the data by molecule identity and excluded 55,267 benchmark molecules (by InChIKey, a fingerprint of chemical identity) from training, so the model couldn’t just memorize the test. I scored three things: whether the SMILES is valid, whether it’s an exact match, and, for wrong answers, how close they are (Tanimoto similarity of fingerprints).

The winner was GLM trained with 70% real images, at 59.8% exact structure on 331 figures from ACS journals. That’s statistically comparable to MolScribe (58.3%), a strong established reader. I wrote more about the real-versus-synthetic story in an earlier note.

Then I got ambitious and tried DPO, a preference-tuning method that teaches a model to prefer good answers over bad ones. The training curves were gorgeous: loss dropped from 0.69 to 0.19, and preference accuracy hit 90–97%. Exact match on the molecules it actually generated was 0–2%. The model had learned to win the preference game, not to read molecules. A second attempt improved validity but still landed at roughly half the accuracy of plain SFT, so I kept SFT and walked away with a lesson I now repeat to anyone who’ll listen: a pretty training score can miss the scientific goal.

VERDICT: four readers, and permission to say “I don’t know”

Once the model could read, the next problem was trust, because on a real page there is no answer key. In my slide comic, the model cheerfully agrees to go label more real drawings in papers, then adds, fairly, that even with high confidence “there is no ground truth. Is it reliable?” That question became VERDICT.

Instead of trusting one model, VERDICT asks four: my fine-tuned VLM plus three open-source readers, DECIMER, MolScribe and MolNexTR, each built differently. It compares their answers by chemical identity (InChIKey), not raw strings, because two different SMILES strings can describe the same molecule. It keeps the disagreements and where each answer came from, and it is allowed to abstain. A real example from my notes: on one FEC image, three readers got it right and one read an F as an I. VERDICT didn’t quietly pick a winner; it kept the 3-to-1 split and showed it.

Agreement turns out to be a very good signal for correctness. It separates right from wrong answers with an AUROC of about 0.916, versus 0.547 for checking how similar a redrawn image looks to the original, which is barely better than a coin flip. I ran VERDICT over about 38K real crops from papers and fed the labels with 3-of-4 agreement back into training. The retraining gains were mixed, so I report data quality and model improvement separately. My slides had a joke here, “99.5% accuracy (reported by me)”, which is exactly the kind of number VERDICT exists to be suspicious of.

Rotation yes, mirror no

My third attempt was to build one piece of chemist common sense straight into the architecture: a rotated drawing is the same molecule. Turn a drawing 30° and nothing about the chemistry changes, but an ordinary CNN has to learn that from data, usually by training on randomly rotated copies. I wanted the model to know it by construction, so it can’t forget. That’s my public research repo, Ouroboros.

There’s a trap, though, and it’s in your hands. Your left and right hands are mirror images: same fingers, same knuckles, yet a left glove won’t fit your right hand. Many molecules come in left- and right-handed versions like this, which chemists call chirality. The two look nearly identical on paper but can behave drastically differently, in a body or in a battery. In drawings, handedness is carried by wedge and dash bonds, the little triangles that say “this bond points toward you” or “away from you.”

So the model should give the same answer when the drawing is rotated, but it must not treat the mirror image as the same molecule. In equivariance jargon, the full group of flat rotations and reflections is called E(2); I deliberately kept only the rotations, a rotation group C_N with no flips (escnn’s rot2dOnR2). In the repo’s mirror test, all 200 of 200 mirrored renderings were labeled as the enantiomer, the mirror-partner molecule, not the original. Left glove, correctly identified.

The image encoder is a steerable CNN over C8, eight discrete rotations 45° apart. Its filters follow known rotation rules, so rotating the image transforms the features in a predictable way instead of scrambling them. That’s exact for 90° rotations, where pixels land back on the pixel grid, and approximate for other angles, because pixels are square and the world isn’t.

The usual move after the encoder would be to squash the features into one token per patch, which throws the direction information away. I kept “position × direction” tokens instead: on a 12×12 grid with 8 directions, that’s 1,152 tokens. Attention between tokens only sees relative position and relative direction, with the relative position written in the asking token’s own direction frame. Rotate the whole picture and the tokens just get relabeled consistently, so nothing about the answer changes. After attention, I average over directions and hand the result to the SMILES decoder.

To test it, the repo has three arms: A, an ordinary CNN; B, the same CNN trained on randomly rotated copies; and C, the C8 steerable CNN plus the rotation-aware token mixer. All three trained on 200,000 synthetic examples. The honest label is that this is a synthetic-data, single-seed research preview. Accuracy on real documents isn’t established yet, and stereochemistry (those wedges again) is still a source of errors.

From a name to a vector

Recognizing a molecule gives you its identity, but a model needs a vector it can compute with, and a molecule can be described in at least three ways. A 1D string is SMILES, a fingerprint or a text description. 2D topology is the graph: which atoms connect to which, and how big the molecule is. 3D geometry is where the atoms actually sit in space, a conformer. It’s like describing a friend by their name, their family tree, or a photo.

Getting from the drawing to the photo is a pipeline: 2D image → SMILES → 3D conformer → energies and forces, computed with machine-learned potentials like MACE and UMA. Rather than invent a new model for the vectors, I started from five public base models, each of which learned about molecules in its own way. Uni-Mol2 hides some atoms and learns to recover them from atoms plus their positions in space. GraphMVP makes the 2D graph and the 3D conformer reconstruct each other. 3D InfoMax pulls a molecule’s graph and 3D views together and pushes different molecules apart. MoleculeSDE generates 3D from 2D and back, plus the same pull-together trick. SMI-TED reads SMILES and learns to rebuild the token sequence.

Then I adapted each of them to my data in three ways. Continued pretraining keeps each model’s own self-supervised objective and simply runs it on my molecules. Scientific property post-training teaches properties I care about: energy, HOMO/LUMO, dipole, volume and electrostatic potential, and for formulations, conductivity, density and viscosity. Cross-view alignment uses InfoNCE, where a 2D view has to pick out its own 3D partner from a crowd of other molecules in the batch.

Five bases times three training types is 15 adaptation runs. The result was refreshingly untidy: no single training type was best for every task. Alignment helped views find each other; property training improved some properties while weakening cross-view matching. You get what you train for, and sometimes you pay for it elsewhere.

Those molecule vectors then become ingredients. A formulation network takes one vector per molecule, plus mixing ratios, salt concentration and temperature, and predicts how the mixture behaves. That’s a first taste of Part 2.

What the extra views really added

With fifteen runs on the table, I wanted an honest answer to a simple question: did the extra views, especially 3D, bring new information, or just more numbers? Most of this section is from my notes and experiments; where I’m thinking out loud instead of reporting a result, I’ll say so.

The 2D graph says which atoms are connected; 3D says how they’re arranged in space. A flexible molecule can keep the same connections and take different shapes, so 3D can add something new. But it can also mostly repeat what 2D already implies, like size and composition. To tell the difference, I compared composition only, 2D, 3D, 2D+3D, and a sneaky control: 2D plus shuffled 3D, where each molecule gets another molecule’s geometry. If the shuffled version helps just as much, the “gain” is a shortcut or just extra dimensions. I also used scaffold-held-out splits, frozen-representation probes, perturbed coordinates and removed inputs. In that scaffold-held-out comparison, real 3D added to 2D cut electronic-energy error by about 18.2% and volume error by about 49.4%. That’s one controlled comparison, not a law for every model and property.

The next thing I learned is that finding a molecule’s other view and predicting its properties are different abilities. Among 5,000 candidates, aligned representations found the matching other view first (R@1) about 0.760 of the time, versus 0.0756 for the base representations and 0.0074 after property training. Property training nearly erased matching.

Copying turned out to be different from understanding, too. A SMILES-only “student” trained to copy a 3D “teacher” matched the teacher’s vectors closely, yet some experimental conductivity tasks didn’t improve. So I tried a branch that keeps the original 2D information while learning geometry. A distance-only 3D branch, which reads distances between atoms but not which elements they are, responds to distance changes but can’t tell every chemical identity, or handedness, apart. And randomly dropping inputs during training mainly helped when 2D was missing at random, not when a whole chemical class was missing or when extrapolating to low temperature.

My conclusion from all of this is to test view matching, teacher matching and property prediction as separate abilities, and to judge an extra data type by whether it helps the actual scientific task, measured against strong single-input models, simple fusion, correct pairs and shuffled pairs.

It helped me to draw how the views relate. The image is how a paper drew the molecule. The text is what the paper says about it. The 1D/2D/3D structure says who is bonded to whom and where the atoms sit. DFT properties are electronic: energies, HOMO/LUMO, how readily it gets reduced. MD properties are collective liquid behavior: solvation, density, diffusion, transport. The molecule’s identity, the InChIKey that VERDICT checks, is the shared key that links all of them, and alignment (InfoNCE) places the views in one shared space. Some information overlaps: 2D and 3D both know composition and size. Some lives in only one view: geometry and stereo in 3D, context and reported use (solvent, salt or additive?) in the text, and collective behavior only in MD.

This next bit is framing rather than a result: a text-only language model sees only what someone wrote down about a molecule, not its geometry or how it moves, and a lot of chemistry never gets written down as sentences. My non-text inputs over the summer were molecular images, atom graphs, 3D coordinates, MD trajectories, simulation-state vectors and experimental numbers. There are several ways to hand them to a model: write the numbers into a prompt as text, use graph encoders, use time or sequence models, project them into an LLM as “soft tokens,” or use retrieval and evidence tools. VERDICT is a verifier of the last kind, built on agreement between independent readers and chemical identity.

I judge each route by whether it helps the target task, and I keep asking what useful information survives compression. Squeezing 5,000 frames into one vector is great, unless the squeeze throws away the physics; a small representation is useless if it lost the essential part. That’s also why my cell assistant in Part 3 shows measured, computed and predicted values separately, along with which records a conclusion used.

A truly multimodal database

All of this pays off in one place: once recognition is reliable, every molecule pulled from a paper becomes an entry in a truly multimodal database. My slide calls it “scientific multi-modal retrieval and alignment”: SMILES and 2D graphs, the image from the paper, the paper’s description, 3D geometry, and non-text values from multi-scale simulations, all linked by the same molecule. Image ↔ text ↔ 3D geometry ↔ DFT ↔ MD.

People use it through the MU product and a Chrome extension, and the point is fast retrieval starting from a picture. From a molecule image you can jump to the paper’s own description of it; to properties computed by DFT, such as its electronic properties and how readily it gets reduced; or to properties computed by MD, such as solvation, density, diffusion and transport.

Notice the last one. MD properties aren’t about a molecule on its own; they’re about what it does in a crowd.

What this got us

By the end of Part 1, a molecule in a paper was no longer just pixels: it had a checked identity, 1D/2D/3D vectors from fifteen adaptation runs, and computed DFT and MD properties, all linked in one database. In hindsight this was the first layer of something bigger, recognize and represent, with a verifier attached. Part 2 takes these molecules and their computed properties, mixes them into electrolytes, and asks the much harder question of how they move.
entry.summary: Part 1, molecules: the first layer everything else in the series builds on. Teaching models to recognize molecules in real papers (hand-drawn ones too), check their own answers, and turn them into vectors and a multimodal database that the electrolytes of Part 2 are later mixed from

entry.title: Real data, not more synthetic data, closes the OCSR gap

link.title: Real data, not more synthetic data, closes the OCSR gap

entry.content:
A short summary of what we found in Real Data Closes Synthetic-to-Real Gap in Optical Chemical Structure Recognition.

Optical chemical structure recognition looks solved if you only test on rendered molecules. The starting recognizer, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, reaches over 91% accuracy on synthetic images — and below 16% on the ACS, CLEF-IP and USPTO benchmarks, which are real document crops. That gap is the whole problem: millions of structures exist only as drawings inside patents and papers.

So we fine-tuned 21 recognizers on mixtures of synthetically rendered structures and labeled real depictions from patents, journal figures and hand-drawn collections, varying three things independently: the base VLM, the fraction of real training data, and whether the vision tower was adapted.

Real data is the variable that matters

For Qwen2.5-VL, ACS exact match goes from 0.15 with no real data, to 0.37 at 9.5% real data, to 0.46 at 50.2%. A tenth of the training mixture being real is worth more than anything else we varied — which is a useful thing to know when labeling real depictions is the expensive part.

Vision-tower LoRA is base-dependent

Adapting the vision tower is usually treated as a knob you turn on. It isn’t:

  • Qwen2.5-VL: +0.00, paired p = 1.00 — no effect at all.
  • InternVL3-8B: +22.8 to +34.6 points.
  • GLM-4.1V-9B: a modest gain.

Same task, same data, opposite conclusions depending on the backbone. Any claim of the form “vision LoRA helps VLM fine-tuning” needs the base model attached to it.

Choose the base and the mixture together

The spread between base models is largest with no real data (0.21) and shrinks to 0.06 at 70% real data — and the ranking changes along the way. Picking a backbone on a synthetic-only ablation and then scaling up real data can leave you on the wrong model.

The strongest recognizer ends at 0.96 exact match on clean renders and 0.49, 0.65, 0.84 and 0.76 on ACS, CLEF-IP, UOB and USPTO respectively. Real documents are still far from solved — which is why the production path we ship, VERDICT, is an ensemble that abstains rather than a single model that always answers.
entry.summary: What 21 fine-tuned recognizers say about mixing synthetic and real training images
